entries.text:
Scientific visualization supports both the inspection of scientific data and the communication of data-derived insights, but translating a data question into a graphic can impose substantial implementation work. Matplotlib is well established in the scientific Python ecosystem and provides fine-grained control over plot objects, their placement, and their appearance. However, its relatively low-level interface makes some common statistical graphics cumbersome. For example, a scatter plot in which marker size encodes a numeric variable and marker shape encodes a categorical variable requires the user to transform size values into graphical units and separately invoke a plotting function for each categorical level. This manual handling can slow exploratory analysis and obscure the correspondence between a dataset and the visual question being examined.

Waskom’s seaborn library addresses this problem through a high-level interface to matplotlib that integrates closely with pandas data structures and exposes a declarative, dataset-oriented API (Waskom, 2021) [JOSS03021]. Given a dataset and a plot specification, seaborn maps data values to visual attributes such as color, size, and style, performs statistical transformations internally, and adds informative axis labels and legends. Its functions can also generate multi-panel figures for comparing conditional subsets or pairings of variables. These mechanisms allow complete graphics to be produced with minimal arguments, supporting rapid prototyping and exploratory data analysis across tabular datasets (Waskom, 2021) [JOSS03021]. The contribution is nevertheless complementary to matplotlib rather than substitutive: seaborn exposes the underlying matplotlib objects, passes customization parameters through to matplotlib functions, and returns axes objects whose limits, ticks, and labels can be adjusted directly. Consequently, seaborn combines opinionated defaults and concise data-oriented specifications with the matplotlib flexibility needed for specialized and publication-quality figures (Waskom, 2021) [JOSS03021].

entries.text: Vallat (2018) presents Pingouin as an open-source Python package intended to partially address the author’s stated gap between Python and R in general statistical analysis [JOSS01026]. In the historical context of the paper, Python is described as rapidly growing because of its ease of use, short learning curve, and extensive data-science and machine-learning package ecosystem, whereas scientists are reported to rely heavily on R for statistical analyses. Pingouin provides accessible functions for several commonly used statistical procedures, including analyses of variance (ANOVAs), analyses of covariance (ANCOVAs), post-hoc tests, non-parametric tests, and effect-size calculations [JOSS01026]. It also includes more advanced procedures, such as Bayesian *t*-tests, repeated-measures correlations, robust correlations, and circular statistics. The package is written in Python 3 and is built largely on the Pandas library, which supports its integration into a data-analysis pipeline [JOSS01026]. This integration situates statistical operations within a tabular data workflow rather than requiring a separate data representation for analysis. Pingouin is accompanied by extensive documentation, an application programming interface, and Jupyter Notebook examples, providing reference material for understanding and applying its functions [JOSS01026]. Thus, Vallat characterizes Pingouin as a Python-based interface to a defined collection of statistical methods, with Pandas serving as the principal foundation for incorporating those methods into broader data-processing workflows.

The comparison between Python and R describes the statistical-software context identified by Vallat at the time of publication and should not be read as a current assessment of either ecosystem.

entries.text: corner.py is a Python module introduced by Foreman-Mackey (2016) for visualizing multidimensional samples with a scatterplot matrix [JOSS00024]. Using matplotlib, the package plots every one- and two-dimensional projection of a sample: one-dimensional projections summarize individual variables, while two-dimensional projections display their joint structure and can reveal covariances [JOSS00024]. The package was originally conceived for inspecting the results of Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations, and its default settings reflect that use case [JOSS00024]. However, corner.py is also intended for displaying many qualitatively different types of samples, making it applicable wherever multidimensional sample structure and pairwise relationships require compact visual inspection [JOSS00024]. The package has been used in astronomical research and has also appeared under the names corner.py and triangle.py [JOSS00024]. Its development occurs on GitHub, while its source code has been archived to Zenodo [JOSS00024]. Thus, corner.py provides a focused visualization mechanism for examining marginal distributions, two-dimensional projections, and covariance patterns in sampled data, without imposing an inferential interpretation on the displayed structures.

entries.text: corner.py is a Python module developed by Foreman-Mackey (2016) for visualizing multidimensional samples through a scatterplot matrix [JOSS00024]. It uses matplotlib to display every one- and two-dimensional projection of a sample: one-dimensional projections summarize the distributions of individual parameters, while two-dimensional projections expose relationships and covariances between parameter pairs. The package was originally conceived for inspecting the results of Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations, and its default settings reflect that use case [JOSS00024]. Its visualization mechanism is nevertheless applicable to samples with qualitatively different origins, making it useful for exploratory analysis of multidimensional distributions beyond MCMC output. corner.py has also been used extensively in astronomical research, where such plots can support the inspection and communication of parameter distributions and covariances [JOSS00024]. The package is developed on GitHub, and its source code has been archived in Zenodo with a DOI; it has also circulated under the names `corner.py` and, previously, `triangle.py` [JOSS00024]. Thus, its contribution is a focused visualization tool for examining multidimensional sample structure through coordinated marginal and pairwise projections.

entries.text:
A central contribution of ArviZ is a common representation and analysis layer for Bayesian model outputs across inference tools. Kumar et al. (2019) distinguish this role from that of probabilistic programming languages (PPLs): systems such as PyStan, PyMC, Edward, emcee, and Pyro are intended to facilitate the construction and solution of Bayesian models, whereas ArviZ is intended to process and analyze the resulting outputs [JOSS01143]. This division preserves the specialization of inference software while providing a shared interface for subsequent statistical and visual work.

The representation is provided by the `InferenceData` class, which stores the different types of data produced by PPLs as labeled `xarray` datasets. Because Bayesian inference naturally produces high-dimensional data, labeled querying, metadata, and efficient algorithms are important for identifying and manipulating particular variables, dimensions, and posterior quantities [JOSS01143]. The datasets can also be stored together using `netCDF4` groups built on HDF5, providing persistent serialization in code and on disk. A single data structure further means that statistical and visualization functions can be implemented once and applied across supported inference outputs, including novel or bespoke Bayesian analyses when they are integrated with ArviZ.

This shared layer connects numerical checks to exploratory visual analysis. ArviZ supports calculation of effective sample size and the R-hat statistic for examining aspects of inference output, as well as PSIS-LOO-CV and WAIC for model comparison [JOSS01143]. It also supplies trace and forest plots, posterior predictive-check plots, pair plots, and parallel-coordinate plots. These tools address distinct tasks: inspecting sampled quantities, comparing parameter estimates, evaluating model predictions, exploring relationships among parameters, and examining model-comparison quantities. More broadly, the library supports inference diagnosis, criticism of model assumptions and predictions, model selection or averaging, and preparation of results for particular audiences [JOSS01143]. The contribution therefore lies in coordinating these numerical and visual analyses around a tool-independent representation, not in replacing probabilistic inference or establishing that any individual diagnostic certifies its quality.

A central contribution of ArviZ is a common representation and analysis layer for Bayesian model outputs produced by different inference tools. Kumar et al. (2019) distinguish this role from that of probabilistic programming languages (PPLs): systems such as PyStan, PyMC, Edward, emcee, and Pyro are intended to facilitate the construction and solution of Bayesian models, whereas ArviZ is intended to process and analyze their results [JOSS01143]. This separation allows inference to remain associated with the computational system that performs it while downstream analysis uses a shared interface.

ArviZ implements this interface through the `InferenceData` class, which stores the different types of data generated by PPLs as labeled xarray datasets. The representation supports labeled querying, efficient algorithms, persistent metadata, and storage through netCDF4 groups built on HDF5, thereby providing serialization for data both in code and on disk [JOSS01143]. Because statistical and visualization functions operate on one common structure, they need not be separately implemented for each inference tool. The same design also supports integration with novel or bespoke Bayesian analyses, within the scope described by the article.

This shared layer connects directly to several numerical and visual tasks that follow inference. Numerical summaries and checks include effective sample size and the R-hat statistic, while model comparison can use Pareto-smoothed importance sampling leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO-CV) and WAIC [JOSS01143]. These functions address inference-quality assessment and comparison, but implementing or calculating a diagnostic does not by itself certify that inference is valid. ArviZ also provides trace and forest plots for examining sampled quantities, posterior predictive-check plots for evaluating predictions, and pair and parallel-coordinate plots for exploring relationships in high-dimensional output. Together, these capabilities support model criticism, comparison, and preparation of results for particular audiences. The contribution is therefore organizational and analytical: it makes heterogeneous Bayesian outputs queryable and inspectable through a common Python layer, without presenting the article as a comparative evaluation of empirical superiority among inference tools [JOSS01143].

entries.text:
Foreman-Mackey et al. (2019) released emcee version 3.0 as a major update to the Python toolkit for affine-invariant ensemble sampling in Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), approximately six years after the previous major release [JOSS01864]. The release delivered a full rewrite of the computational backend, several quality-of-life improvements, and new interfaces for storing sampling results and selecting ensemble proposals [JOSS01864]. A progress bar based on `tqdm` was added as a usability improvement [JOSS01864].

The backends interface enabled real-time serialization of sampling results. As in the original implementation, emcee retained in-memory storage by default; version 3.0 additionally provided an `HDFBackend` class, which serializes the chain to disk through `h5py` [JOSS01864]. Thus, the interface supported persistence during sampling while preserving the existing in-memory behavior.

The principal functional addition was the moves interface. Whereas earlier emcee implementations used the affine-invariant stretch move proposed by Goodman and Weare (2010), version 3.0 allowed users to select among multiple ensemble proposals and to define custom proposals [JOSS01864]. The release included the stretch move, differential evolution and differential evolution snooker update moves, and a kernel density proposal based on the implementation in `kombine` [JOSS01864]. This expansion addressed the documented observation that proposals other than the stretch move may perform better for certain applications [JOSS01864]. The source does not report a universal or numerical benchmark advantage for any move, so the release should be characterized as providing broader proposal support rather than establishing across-application performance superiority. The publication also documented community contributions to emcee and provided citation credit to academic contributors [JOSS01864].

entries.text:
Foreman-Mackey et al. (2019) reported version 3.0 of `emcee`, the first major release of the Python ensemble-sampling toolkit in approximately six years [JOSS01864]. The release delivered a full rewrite of the computational backend, several quality-of-life improvements, and new interfaces for storing sampling results and selecting ensemble proposals [JOSS01864]. The documented usability improvement included a progress bar based on `tqdm` [JOSS01864].

The backends interface added real-time serialization of sampling results. Sampling output remained stored in memory by default, as in the original implementation, while the new `HDFBackend` serialized chains to disk through `h5py` [JOSS01864]. This functionality distinguishes result persistence from the sampler’s computational execution: users could retain the in-memory behavior or write the evolving chain to an HDF5-backed store [JOSS01864].

The principal functional addition was the moves interface. Earlier versions implemented the affine-invariant stretch move proposed by Goodman and Weare; version 3.0 generalized proposal selection by including multiple ensemble moves and an interface for defining custom proposals [JOSS01864]. The supplied implementations comprised the stretch move, differential-evolution and differential-evolution snooker-update moves, and a kernel-density proposal based on the implementation in `kombine` [JOSS01864]. This extension addressed the documented limitation that alternative ensemble proposals may perform better for certain applications [JOSS01864].

These changes constitute delivered library features rather than measured experimental outcomes. The source reports no universal performance improvement and provides no numerical benchmark demonstrating that version 3.0, or any included move, dominates alternatives across applications [JOSS01864]. It instead characterizes the moves interface as enabling proposal choice and customization in settings where performance depends on the application [JOSS01864].

entries.text:
Terpilowski (2019) presents scikit-posthocs as a Python package for conducting multiple pairwise post hoc comparisons after a statistically significant parametric or nonparametric analysis-of-variance result. Its purpose is to help statisticians, data scientists, and researchers assess differences between group levels within a statistical analysis workflow [JOSS01169]. The paper situates the package in a Python ecosystem that lacked implementations of post hoc tests for factorial and block-design data, while SciPy provided individual Student, Wilcoxon, and Mann-Whitney tests that were not adapted to multiple pairwise comparisons. Although statsmodels included TukeyHSD, additional actions were required to integrate it smoothly into an analysis pipeline [JOSS01169].

The package includes parametric pairwise procedures such as Scheffe, Student T, Tamhane T2, and TukeyHSD. It also provides nonparametric methods for factorial designs, including Conover, Dunn, Dwass-Steel-Critchlow-Fligner, Mann-Whitney, Nashimoto-Wright, Nemenyi, van Waerden, and Wilcoxon tests. For block designs, it implements Conover, Durbin and Conover, Miller, Nemenyi, Quade, and Siegel tests. Additional procedures include the Anderson-Darling, Mack-Wolfe, and Hayter tests [JOSS01169]. These methods support pairwise assessment following an omnibus result; they do not entail that every group pair will be statistically significant.

scikit-posthocs also contains outlier-detection procedures based on the interquartile range, Grubbs, Tietjen-Moore, and generalized extreme Studentized deviate tests. The package provides heatmap plots for presenting pairwise-comparison results, but these visualizations summarize statistical outcomes rather than establish or prove a hypothesis. At the time of publication, it was compatible with Python 2 and 3, integrated with Pandas and NumPy, and relied substantially on statsmodels, SciPy, and PMCMRplus. It was fully documented and accompanied by a Jupyter notebook example [JOSS01169].

entries.text:
Terpilowski (2019) presents scikit-posthocs as a Python package for conducting multiple pairwise comparison tests after a statistically significant parametric or nonparametric analysis of variance (ANOVA). Its purpose is to help statisticians, data scientists, and researchers assess differences between group levels while addressing a gap in the Python ecosystem, which at the time lacked implementations of post hoc tests for factorial and block-design data. Although SciPy provided individual Student, Wilcoxon, and Mann–Whitney tests, these tests were not adapted to multiple pairwise comparisons, and the TukeyHSD implementation in Statsmodels required additional steps for integration into an analysis pipeline [JOSS01169].

The package includes parametric procedures such as Scheffe, Student T, Tamhane T2, and TukeyHSD, together with nonparametric tests for factorial designs, including Conover, Dunn, Dwass–Steel–Critchlow–Fligner, Mann–Whitney, Nemenyi, van Waerden, and Wilcoxon tests. It also implements nonparametric procedures for block designs, including Durbin and Conover, Miller, Quade, Siegel, and related tests, as well as Anderson–Darling, Mack–Wolfe, and Hayter tests [JOSS01169]. These functions provide alternative procedures suited to different designs and distributional assumptions; they do not imply that every significant omnibus result yields significant differences for every pair.

In addition, scikit-posthocs supplies outlier-detection algorithms based on the interquartile range, Grubbs, Tietjen–Moore, and generalized extreme Studentized deviate tests. Its plotting functionality presents pairwise-comparison results as heatmaps or significance plots, which summarize test outcomes rather than establish hypotheses independently. The package supports Python 2 and 3, integrates with Pandas and NumPy, and extends functionality from Statsmodels, SciPy, and PMCMRplus [JOSS01169].
